readings.title: Ethan Frome: Denis Eady’s cutter and the walk home
readings.challenge: Separate what Ethan actually sees and hears from his hiding place from what he hopes it means.
readings.focus: A hidden watcher, a rival, and the small signs from which Ethan builds his hope.
readings.context: Edith Wharton’s Ethan Frome (1911) is set in Starkfield, a poor hill village in western Massachusetts. Ethan Frome, a farmer married to the ailing Zeena, has come to walk home her young cousin Mattie Silver, who lives with them as unpaid help, after a church dance; he has just watched her dancing with Denis Eady, the grocer’s son. A cutter is a light one-horse sleigh, a storm-door an outer wooden porch built against winter wind, and coasting is sledding downhill.
readings.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. The narrator’s descriptions and historical assumptions invite scrutiny.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, from the dancers leaving the church hall through the talk about the big elm; opens “AS the dancers poured out of the hall Frome, drawing back behind the projecting…”; closes “…tossed back, almost indifferently; and suddenly she began to walk on with a rapid step.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Ethan stay hidden behind the storm-door instead of making himself known? What does he gain by watching, and what does it cost him?
facilitatorNotes: Shyness pulls him “into the dark angle of the wall,” and he will not signal to her “for the world”: hiding lets him see whether Mattie chooses Denis without his pressure. The cost is that he becomes “the hidden watcher,” tortured by a choice he cannot influence. Some readers will call this cowardice, others a wish to know her free choice; the text supports both.
evidence: A wave of shyness pulled him back into the dark angle of the wall
Not for the world would he have made a sign to her

questions.prompt: Mattie refuses Denis’s ride. How does the narration make us read her refusal only through Ethan’s eyes and hopes?
facilitatorNotes: Ethan notices that she “no longer turned her head,” then follows a “pantomime” of silhouettes beyond earshot. He reads gestures in the dark, not words, and his heart swings “out over a black void” and back. Her refusal could be loyalty to Ethan, teasing of Denis, or simple caution on an icy night (“Not on such a night”); the passage leaves room for each.
evidence: Frome noticed that she no longer turned her head from side to side
he could only follow the shadowy pantomime of their silhouettes

questions.prompt: Ned Hale and Ruth Varnum nearly ran into “the big elm.” How do Mattie’s remarks about the engaged couple and the elm work on Ethan, and on a reader who has read the novel’s opening frame?
facilitatorNotes: Ethan hears “They’re so happy!” as if she meant herself and him, and boasts he can steer her past the tree, knowing he is “talking big.” For a reader who has seen the disabled Ethan of twenty-four years later, the elm that “ought to be cut down” reads as an omen. The same words hold hope for Ethan and dread for the reader.
evidence: made the words sound as if she had been thinking of herself and him
The elm is dangerous, though. It ought to be cut down,

readings.title: Ethan Frome: an evening by the stove (Chapter V)
readings.challenge: Notice how objects in the kitchen (a rocking-chair, the cat, a strip of sewing) carry feelings the characters never say aloud.
readings.focus: A marriage imagined in one ordinary evening, and the absent wife who still occupies the room.
readings.context: Edith Wharton’s Ethan Frome (1911) is set in Starkfield, a poor hill village in western Massachusetts. Recap: Ethan’s wife Zeena has gone overnight to Bettsbridge to see a new doctor, leaving Ethan alone with her cousin Mattie Silver, who works in the house for her keep. At supper the cat broke Zeena’s treasured red pickle-dish, which Mattie had taken down to make the table pretty; Ethan laid the pieces back on the shelf, meaning to glue them before Zeena noticed. Coasting is sledding; “stuff” here is cloth.
readings.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. The narrator’s descriptions and historical assumptions invite scrutiny.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, the whole chapter; opens “THEY finished supper, and while Mattie cleared the table Ethan went to look at the cows…”; closes “…door of her room had closed on her he remembered that he had not even touched her hand.”.

questions.prompt: What happens when Mattie sits in Zeena’s rocking-chair, and why can neither of them stay comfortable with it?
facilitatorNotes: Ethan sees “the face of the superseded woman” blot out Mattie’s, and Mattie moves back, saying she cannot see to sew. Later the cat leaves the chair and it rocks by itself. The chair keeps Zeena present in her absence; readers may read it as guilt, or as the household’s order resisting the pair.
evidence: It was almost as if the other face, the face of the superseded woman, had obliterated that of the intruder.
the empty chair had set up a spectral rocking

questions.prompt: Why does ordinary talk give Ethan “an illusion of long-established intimacy” that no outburst could? Is the narrator sharing the illusion or exposing it?
facilitatorNotes: Talk about snow, sociables and village quarrels is what a settled couple shares, so it lets him imagine they “would always go on doing so.” The words “illusion” and “fiction” keep the narrator at a distance even while the prose lingers lovingly on the scene; the trailing dots let the dream run on.
evidence: produced in Ethan an illusion of long-established intimacy
he set his imagination adrift on the fiction that they had always spent their evenings thus

questions.prompt: Ethan kisses only “the bit of stuff in his hold,” and the chapter ends: “he had not even touched her hand.” What does this restraint suggest about him and about the “warm lamplit room”?
facilitatorNotes: Out of doors the night before he had put his arm about her; indoors, with its “ancient implications of conformity and order,” she seems unapproachable, and his desire goes into the cloth. The restraint can be read as decency, timidity or the weight of convention, and the last sentence as regret or relief; ask readers to choose and defend a reading.
evidence: with all its ancient implications of conformity and order
he remembered that he had not even touched her hand

readings.title: Ethan Frome: glue, sleet and Zeena’s return (Chapter VI)
readings.challenge: Follow a chain of small delays and decide how much is chance and how much Ethan’s own choosing.
readings.focus: Ordinary bad luck tightening into dread, with the village watching.
readings.context: Recap: with Zeena away, Ethan and Mattie spent a quiet evening by the stove, both aware it might be the only one; he never touched her. The broken pickle-dish still sits hidden on its shelf, and Ethan must buy glue before Zeena returns. Jotham Powell is a hired man; the Flats is the railway station; a sledge is a heavy sled for hauling logs, and teaming is hauling with a pair of horses.
readings.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. The narrator’s descriptions and historical assumptions invite scrutiny.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, the whole chapter; opens “THE next morning at breakfast Jotham Powell was between them, and Ethan tried to hide his…”; closes “…then she said, as she had said the night before: "I guess it's about time for supper."”.

questions.prompt: List what goes wrong between breakfast and evening. Which of these delays could Ethan have avoided?
facilitatorNotes: Ice, the gray’s cut knee, sleet, slow loading, no glue at Eady’s and a long search at the widow Homan’s. Most are weather and chance, but Ethan chooses to lead the injured horse home and wash the cut himself, and to send Jotham to meet Zeena. The narrator’s “grim flash of self-derision” looks back on how much he staked on these odds.
evidence: but everything went wrong from the start
He remembered afterward, with a grim flash of self-derision, what importance he had attached to the weighing of these probabilities

questions.prompt: What do the scenes at Eady’s store and the widow Homan’s add to the chapter besides delay?
facilitatorNotes: Denis and “the golden youth of Starkfield” mock Ethan, and the widow asks “sympathetic questions” before calling out a guess that is uncomfortably close to the truth. Starkfield notices everything; the parting line is dramatic irony, since the reader knows exactly what has been broken.
evidence: They hailed Ethan with ironic compliment and offers of conviviality
I hope Zeena ain't broken anything she sets store by,

questions.prompt: Why does Jotham’s refusal of supper seem “ominous” to Ethan, and what might Jotham know?
facilitatorNotes: Jotham is “seldom loth” to take a free meal, so his repeated “I guess I’ll go along back” suggests that something on the drive from the Flats made him want to avoid the house, perhaps Zeena’s mood or her plans. It could also be simple tact. The chapter closes on Mattie’s words from the night before, now heavy with threat.
evidence: To Ethan there was something vaguely ominous in this stolid rejection of free food and warmth
I guess it's about time for supper.

readings.title: Ethan Frome: “complications” and a hired girl (Chapter VII, first part)
readings.challenge: Watch power shift in a dialogue: who asks, who answers, and who finally decides.
readings.focus: Illness as a claim to authority, and the first open quarrel of a seven-year marriage.
readings.context: Recap: Zeena has come home from the new doctor and gone straight to her room. Ethan has the glue but has not mended the dish. Two days earlier, to avoid driving Zeena to the station, he told her that Andrew Hale would pay him cash for lumber. Mattie, Zeena’s orphaned cousin, has no money and nowhere else to live. An almshouse is a public home for the destitute; to foist is to force something unwanted on someone.
readings.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. This chapter includes a bitter marital quarrel and a moment when Ethan’s hatred clenches his fist against his wife.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, from Ethan going up to Zeena’s room through his leaving it; opens “ETHAN went out into the passage to hang up his wet garments. He listened for Zeena's step…”; closes “…the bed a little while," she answered mildly; and he turned and walked out of the room.”.

questions.prompt: How does the word “complications” work in Starkfield, according to the narrator, and what does Zeena gain by claiming it?
facilitatorNotes: Everybody has “troubles”; “only the chosen” have “complications,” which are a distinction and usually a death-warrant. The narrator’s dry tone mocks this ranking of illness, and Zeena speaks like one “singled out for a great fate.” Whether she is truly very ill the novel never settles; readers can argue it either way.
evidence: only the chosen had "complications."
as of one consciously singled out for a great fate

questions.prompt: “Ethan had no suppleness in deceiving.” Trace how his earlier lie about Andrew Hale’s payment turns against him.
facilitatorNotes: Zeena uses the promised fifty dollars to show a girl is affordable; Ethan must call his own story “a misunderstanding.” Caught in a lie for the first time, he loses the argument’s footing, and she moves to her real aim: Mattie’s board saved.
evidence: Ethan had no suppleness in deceiving.
I guess that was a misunderstanding,

questions.prompt: As Ethan grows furious, Zeena grows “mild” and “level.” Who wins this scene, and is the narrator’s picture of Zeena as “an evil energy” fair?
facilitatorNotes: She wins: she lets him “feel the full force of the contrast” between his excitement and her composure, and he ends by asking a feeble question. The “evil energy” is Ethan’s loathing filtered through the narration; Zeena has her own grievances (her lost health, a year of keeping a penniless cousin). Readers should test his view against what she actually says.
evidence: as if giving him time to feel the full force of the contrast between his own excitement and her composure
Now she had mastered him and he abhorred her.

readings.title: Ethan Frome: the kiss and the pickle-dish (Chapter VII, end)
readings.challenge: Read a scene in which a broken object carries more meaning than anything the characters say about themselves.
readings.focus: Desire finally spoken, and Zeena’s grief for a dish she never used.
readings.context: Recap: Zeena has announced that the new doctor forbids her housework, that she has hired a girl from Bettsbridge, and that Mattie must leave to make room. Ethan, exposed in a lie about money, could not stop her. Mattie does not know yet; she has supper waiting downstairs. Stamford, Connecticut, is the town Mattie came from. Text note: the 1911 first printing used here left a blank where type failed to print; this night supplies ‘l’ in “small” from Scribner’s Modern Student’s Library printing (copyright 1911, 1922).
readings.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. This chapter shows a married man kissing his wife’s young cousin, and a wife’s bitter accusation of the girl.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, from Ethan coming down to supper to the end of the chapter; opens “In the kitchen Mattie was sitting by the stove, the cat curled up on her knees. She…”; closes “…up the bits of broken glass she went out of the room as if she carried a dead body . . .”.

questions.prompt: How does Mattie learn that she must leave, and what does the image of a “torch of warning” suggest about that moment?
facilitatorNotes: Ethan kisses her and then cries “You can’t go, Matt!”, so his protest announces the news he meant to soften. The torch passed “through a black landscape” makes the words a danger signal lighting up a future she has not let herself see.
evidence: as though a torch of warning flew from hand to hand through a black landscape
Must I go?

questions.prompt: Mattie thinks she might find work at Stamford; Ethan imagines “the million bread-seekers of the cities.” What future does each foresee for her?
facilitatorNotes: She speaks “as if knowing that he knew she had no hope”; he remembers the faces of girls in Worcester whose lives began hopefully, a hint of poverty or worse. The novel shows how few paths were open to a young woman without training, money or friends.
evidence: among the million bread-seekers of the cities
as if knowing that he knew she had no hope

questions.prompt: Why does Zeena care so much about a pickle-dish she never used, and how does she turn its breaking into a judgment on Mattie?
facilitatorNotes: It was a wedding present, put away “o’ purpose when we was married” and never used, even for the minister, so it can stand for the marriage itself: kept, untouched, sterile. She links Mattie’s act to her father’s ruin and carries the pieces out “as if she carried a dead body.” Ethan’s “The cat done it” and Mattie’s honest confession are worth comparing; some readers will also feel Zeena’s tears are real grief.
evidence: I put Aunt Philura Maple's pickle-dish up there o' purpose when we was married
as if she carried a dead body

readings.title: Ethan Frome: a letter he cannot afford to send (Chapter VIII, first part)
readings.challenge: Follow a mind arguing with itself, and mark the exact fact that ends the argument.
readings.focus: Escape imagined in detail, then cancelled by money.
readings.context: Edith Wharton’s Ethan Frome (1911) is set in Starkfield, a poor hill village in western Massachusetts. Recap: Ethan’s wife Zeena has dismissed her cousin Mattie Silver, the young woman Ethan loves, to make room for a hired girl, and after finding her treasured pickle-dish broken she called Mattie a bad girl. Mattie leaves tomorrow. Ethan’s “study” is a cold back room he fitted up when his father’s illness called him home from a year’s course at a technological college in Worcester. To go West was to start again in the newer states; alimony is money a divorced husband pays his former wife. Text note: the 1911 first printing used here left a blank where type failed to print; this night supplies ‘c’ in “spectral” from Scribner’s Modern Student’s Library printing (copyright 1911, 1922).
readings.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. Ethan plans to desert his sick wife; the passage presents his reasoning without endorsing it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, from Ethan’s study through the moonrise; opens “WHEN Ethan was called back to the farm by his father's illness his mother gave him, for…”; closes “…as though all the beauty of the night had been poured out to mock his wretchedness . . .”.

questions.prompt: What do the study’s furnishings tell us about the young man Ethan hoped to be?
facilitatorNotes: Shelves of books, a Lincoln engraving, a calendar of “Thoughts from the Poets”: he tried to copy the study of a minister who lent him books. The room is now unusable because he gave Mattie its stove. Zeena’s engagement cushion, which he flings across the floor, belongs to the same lost past.
evidence: tried, with these meagre properties to produce some likeness to the study of a "minister"
the only piece of needlework he had ever seen her do

questions.prompt: The story of the man “over the mountain” seems to prove that running away works. What does Ethan leave out when he tells it to himself?
facilitatorNotes: In that tale everyone prospers, even “the deserted wife.” Ethan’s farm and mill are “mortgaged to the limit,” Zeena could not work them, and he cannot even pay the fares. The facts arrive one at a time, each closing an exit, until the advertisement of “Reduced Rates” shows him he cannot afford the reduced rate.
evidence: The deserted wife had not done badly either.
Farm and mill were mortgaged to the limit of their value

questions.prompt: The moon rises on “the night on which he was to have taken Mattie coasting.” How does the moonlit landscape answer his despair?
facilitatorNotes: The scene seems “poured out to mock his wretchedness,” coming just after the image of “prison-warders hand-cuffing a convict.” Ethan reads nature as mockery; a reader may see it as indifferent beauty that only feels cruel to a prisoner. Both readings depend on the window he looks through.
evidence: like prison-warders hand-cuffing a convict
it seemed as though all the beauty of the night had been poured out to mock his wretchedness

readings.title: Ethan Frome: Mrs. Hale’s kindness (Chapter VIII, end)
readings.challenge: Find the moment a character sees his own plan in plain words, and what makes him see it.
readings.focus: Sympathy that wakes a conscience: kindness blocks a dishonest plan.
readings.context: Recap: Ethan spent the night in his cold study drafting a letter to tell Zeena he would go West, until he saw he had no money even for the fares. Mattie found him there at dawn. Andrew Hale, a Starkfield builder, owes Ethan for lumber; Mrs. Hale is his wife. Lumbago is back pain; huckabuck is a coarse towelling; a match-safe is a box for matches. Text note: the 1911 first printing used here left blanks where type failed to print; this night supplies ‘e’ in “like” and ‘y’ in “you’ll” from Scribner’s Modern Student’s Library printing (copyright 1911, 1922).
readings.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. The narrator’s descriptions and historical assumptions invite scrutiny.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, from Ethan waking in the study to the end of the chapter; opens “He fell asleep, and when he woke the chill of the winter dawn was in the room. He felt…”; closes “He turned and walked slowly back to the farm.”.

questions.prompt: Morning briefly persuades Ethan that “things’ll straighten out.” Which details show how fragile that hope is?
facilitatorNotes: The warm kitchen and Mattie’s familiar work make her leaving seem “impossible,” but Jotham at once repeats Zeena’s exact arrangements: the trunk at noon, the new girl at five, the six o’clock train. Zeena’s brisk “alertness and activity” at breakfast confirms that nothing has softened.
evidence: made it seem impossible that she should ever cease to be a part of the scene
Mis' Frome said the new girl'd be at the Flats at five

questions.prompt: Zeena wants to “go over things” with Mattie: a missing towel, a match-safe. What does this inventory add to the dismissal?
facilitatorNotes: It treats Mattie like a departing servant suspected of taking things, in an “unperturbed voice,” while Mattie can only say she is “much obliged.” Zeena’s remark that plants “pine away when they ain’t cared for” may glance at Mattie, or at Zeena herself; readers can weigh both.
evidence: I know there's a huckabuck towel missing
they pine away when they ain't cared for

questions.prompt: Why do Mrs. Hale’s words, “You’ve had an awful mean time, Ethan Frome,” stop him from asking the Hales for money?
facilitatorNotes: Her pity makes him feel less alone and then lets him see his plan plainly: to obtain money “on false pretences” from kind people and leave Zeena destitute. “The madness fell.” Readers can argue whether this is moral clarity or defeat; the paragraph’s plain sentence about a poor man and a sickly wife holds both.
evidence: He was planning to take advantage of the Hales' sympathy to obtain money from them on false pretences.
the madness fell and he saw his life before him as it was

readings.title: Ethan Frome: the trunk and the last dinner (Chapter IX, first part)
readings.challenge: Watch how one repeated sentence becomes a small act of rebellion.
readings.focus: Ethan’s defiance in words, and Zeena’s in housekeeping.
readings.context: Recap: Ethan walked to Starkfield meaning to ask Andrew Hale for an advance so that he could run away West with Mattie, but Mrs. Hale’s kindness showed him the plan was a fraud, and he turned home. Mattie leaves this afternoon; Zeena has arranged for Jotham Powell to drive her to the station at the Flats, and Daniel Byrne to carry her trunk. Text note: the 1911 first printing used here left a blank where type failed to print; this night supplies ‘r’ in “repeated” from Scribner’s Modern Student’s Library printing (copyright 1911, 1922).
readings.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. The narrator’s descriptions and historical assumptions invite scrutiny.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, from Daniel Byrne’s sleigh at the kitchen door through Ethan harnessing the sorrel; opens “AT the kitchen door Daniel Byrne sat in his sleigh behind a big-boned gray who pawed the…”; closes “…in the same way; and one by one all the days between rose up and stood before him . . .”.

questions.prompt: What does Mattie’s emptied room look like, and why does Ethan remember its earlier state so exactly?
facilitatorNotes: He had been in it only once, yet recalls the quilt, the pin-cushion and her mother’s photograph; now it is as bare as on her arrival. The precise memory shows how much attention he has paid her; the bareness makes her going real before anyone says so.
evidence: Now these and all other tokens of her presence had vanished
as bare and comfortless as when Zeena had shown her into it on the day of her arrival

questions.prompt: Ethan says three times that he will drive Mattie himself. What exactly is he defying, and how much does the defiance change?
facilitatorNotes: He overrides Zeena’s plan and her excuse about the stove in Mattie’s room, his first open resistance. But he fights only for the drive, not for Mattie’s staying; Zeena keeps her “monotonous mildness” and gets the rest. Readers may see courage, or a gesture that costs Zeena nothing.
evidence: I'm going to drive her over myself.
Zeena persisted with the same monotonous mildness

questions.prompt: Harnessing the sorrel, Ethan remembers fetching Mattie from the Flats “little more than a year ago.” How does this memory frame the afternoon ahead?
facilitatorNotes: The same soft weather and the same horse make the drive that began their story the drive that will end it. The days between “rose up and stood before him” like ghosts, and the trailing dots leave a reader uneasy about what he means to do.
evidence: he remembered the day when he had made the same preparations
one by one all the days between rose up and stood before him

readings.title: Ethan Frome: Shadow Pond (Chapter IX, the drive)
readings.challenge: Read a farewell in which the most important things are first said indirectly and then said outright.
readings.focus: Memory, confession, and a wish for death spoken aloud.
readings.context: Recap: over Zeena’s objection, Ethan is driving Mattie to the evening train himself. The night before, he began a letter telling Zeena he would go West, then left it unfinished in his study. Shadow Pond, in the woods off the Bettsbridge road, is where they met at a church picnic the previous summer.
readings.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. In this passage Ethan says he would almost rather Mattie were dead than married to someone else, and she says she wishes she were dead.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, from Ethan finding Mattie in his study through their talk on the road home; opens “He flung the bearskin into the sleigh, climbed to the seat, and drove up to the house.…”; closes “"Yes; but it's true just the same."”.

questions.prompt: Mattie is “just taking a look round” Ethan’s study. Why might she go there, and what does the drive later reveal?
facilitatorNotes: She is saying goodbye to his room, and perhaps looking for something of his. On the road she produces the unfinished letter: she knows he wanted to leave Zeena for her. Her “wavering smile” hid a discovery.
evidence: I was just taking a look round—that's all
it was the letter to his wife that he had begun the night before and forgotten to destroy

questions.prompt: At Shadow Pond Ethan has “the illusion that he was a free man.” How do the place and the memory of the picnic create that illusion, and what ends it?
facilitatorNotes: The fallen log, the locket, the pink hat recall “inarticulate flashes” of happiness, “a butterfly in the winter woods.” Mattie ends the moment herself (“We mustn’t stay here any longer”), and the sunset turning the pine-boles “from red to gray” marks the change.
evidence: as if they had surprised a butterfly in the winter woods
We mustn't stay here any longer.

questions.prompt: “I’d a’most rather have you dead than that!” and “Oh, I wish I was.” How should a reader take these lines, knowing that the next scene is on School House Hill?
facilitatorNotes: Ethan’s jealousy of an imagined husband turns into a death wish he is at once ashamed of; Mattie answers with despair she has felt “every minute of the day.” The lines prepare the decision on the hill without stating it. Some readers hear tragic love; others hear possessiveness in Ethan’s words. Both can be argued from the exchange.
evidence: I'd a'most rather have you dead than that!
I've been wishing it every minute of the day.
